title: Steering an LLM AutoResearch Loop with Domain Context: A Case Study with Vehicle Energy Models
abstract: Research Software Engineers (RSEs) often work with Machine Learning (ML) models integratedinto scientific software stacks, and incremental model improvements are valuable but expensivein human time and attention. Our team maintains RouteE-Powertrain, which predicts vehicleenergy consumption and is integrated into RouteE-Compass for energy-aware routing.We investigated whether a Large Language Model (LLM) agent could help accelerate thediscovery process for model improvements by taking on certain elements that are challengingfor us, like context switching and managing limited time budgets. We began with an existingautomated research harness (Andrej Karpathy's autoresearch) where an agent canrepeatedly modify the model and then evaluate against a held-out dataset. This harness foundlarge improvements in our error metrics, but upon further inspection, the winning model wasunusable in our application domain. Specifically, it used unobservable future road network linkstates that are not compatible with our energy-aware route planning application and yielded avery large compute cost at inference time, leading to prohibitive computational overhead forroute planning. We also identified the need for additional agent instruction around logging,single-variable experimentation, token accounting, and trial budgets to support improvedanalysis. We accumulated these discoveries into a modified harness that would guide the agentwithin our narrower optimization space.We then ran two sessions over the same modified harness, each ~50 trials, ~8 hours wall time,~$35 token cost. The first session included our complete modified harness, whereas the secondsession excluded only the domain-specific guidance. Both sessions were then audited in anenvironment where only valid input features were used, for one million model evaluations. Theunguided experiment chose a final model of an ensemble of 75% GBDT/25% CNN and reporteda better overall RMSE score, but when audited, the model performed even worse than thebaseline and took 951 seconds to run one million evaluations (0.95ms/eval). The domain-guidedexperiment produced a 2x128 MLP with a properly constrained feature set which reduced ournetwork link-level RMSE by 49% and completed the audit in 1.4 seconds (0.0014ms/eval).Grounding the agent with explicit deployment constraints ensured that all improvementsremained usable in our application, highlighting that human-in-the-loop domain context is criticalfor this type of automated discovery.We have open sourced the modified harness, along with the archive of the two experimentsessions, with the hope that this will be a valuable resource for other RSE teams whomaintain ML models.

title: LLM-assisted relevance screening of EU research projects for the TRIMIS transport database – validation outputs and analysis code
abstract: This dataset contains the outputs used to evaluate how well large language models (LLMs) can identify transport-relevant research projects for TRIMIS, the European Commission's Transport Research and Innovation Monitoring and Information System. A random sample of 250 Horizon Europe projects from CORDIS was labelled by domain experts as not relevant, partly relevant or relevant to transport. The same projects were then scored by four open-weight LLMs, each run with 13 different prompts, giving 52 sets of results. Each file lists, per project, the expert label, the model's score, its justification and supporting quotation, and processing cost. The package also includes the prompts, a Python script that recomputes all reported statistics, and the resulting tables and charts. It supports the article "Enhancing Transport Innovation Knowledge Management Workflows Using Artificial Intelligence: A TRIMIS Database Case Study" (European Transport Research Review, 2026).

title: [Design and implementation of a clinical trial image medical record desensitization system based on artificial intelligence technology].
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To designe a clinical trial image medical record desensitization system based on artificial intelligence technology and to conduct preliminary applications, achieving the protection of patient privacy and promoting the safe use of clinical image data in clinical trial projects. METHODS: The clinical trial image record desensitization system based on artificial intelligence technology was first performed to preprocess operations, such as cropping and compression on medical images to initialize the image records. Then, it utilized advanced image recognition, natural language processing, and convolutional neural network technologies to automatically classify (labeled, feature extraction, and text recognition) according to the content of medical documents. It automatically identified sensitive information in the image records of clinical trial patients, including personal identity information such as patient name, identification number, medical record number, phone number, and birthplace. Pixel-level masking or blurring was performed on the identified sensitive information points, and an artificial online desensitization system based on canvas technology was assisted to ensure the security and confidentiality of privacy data. RESULTS: The designed clinical trial image record desensitization system exhibited high performance and efficiency in both desensitization effect and processing speed. After desensitizing 100 000 pieces of image record data in this system, a total of 9 000 medical record image samples were randomly selected from the processed medical document types for automated desensitization effect verification. The average accuracy rate of medical document desensitization reached 88.48%, with an accuracy rate of up to 99.40% for serious adverse event medical documents. CONCLUSION: The clinical trial image record desensitization system based on artificial intelligence technology improves accuracy and efficiency in medical data privacy protection. Combined with the artificial online desensitization auxiliary system, it can be applied in production environments, providing reliable technical support for the safe sharing and effective utilization of clinical trial image records.

title: Research Package: Mitigation of Cross-Subspace Semantic Bleed in High-Dimensional Transformer and Latent Diffusion Architectures
abstract: Contains the theoretical paper formalizing Cross-Subspace Semantic Bleed (CSSB) along with an automated PyTorch/Hugging Face validation framework script. CSSB occurs when high-dimensional transformer matrices inadvertently map semantically unrelated domains into overlapping vector trajectories, leading to hidden downstream reasoning degradation or alignment drift. The provided pipeline implements Layer-wise Linear Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) scanning [cite: 1], multi-step Shannon entropy tracking [cite: 1], and causal null-space ablation interventions (\(P = I - vv^T\)) to mitigate cross-attention attribute binding and linear refusal circuit interference.

title: The Changing Architecture of Intellectual Property in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly encompassing industries and systems of governance, increasing efficiency, automation, and innovation. It has become a vital tool for creating text, images, music, software, and potentially patentable inventions. This rapid advancement in IP is not without risks at every stage of the innovation cycle. Traditional IP regimes arise from human creativity and invention, while AI performs activities traditionally attributed to both. India doesn't have any regulatory framework on AI-generated intellectual property, yet the Copyright Act, 1957, and Patents Act, 1970, contain certain principles—an answer to several emerging questions. This article argues that India should adopt a balanced approach to AI-generated creations instead of granting independent IP rights or prohibiting them. Instead, it should adopt a model that will protect creative human contribution as well as hold AI developers accountable for unlawful acquisition and exploitation of protected works.

title: Break-even analysis of risk-based trade screening: per-route test scores and analysis code (reproducibility materials)
abstract: Reproducibility materials for the article "When Screening Does Not Pay: Break-Even Conditions for Risk-Based Trade Inspection under Extreme Class Imbalance" by Sushanta Paul (National Board of Revenue, Bangladesh). Contents: (1) per-route test scores of five detectors (interpretable triadic residual, its logistic readout, local outlier factor, isolation forest, gradient boosting) with injected-anomaly labels for 7,637,362 candidate routes, one training seed, deposited in 15 parts with SHA-256 checksums; (2) analysis scripts that compute the exact operating characteristic, break-even hurdle, optimal inspection budgets, a negative-subsampling prevalence test, a test-set bootstrap, and the figures; (3) the exact result tables. See README.md for reassembly and run order. The scores were generated with the code of the triadic trade-anomaly screening benchmark (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20513788), built from public UN Comtrade and CEPII GeoDist data.

title: Qstreams: Role-Biased Residual Streams for Transformers — Reproducibility Package
abstract: Source code and saved-result reproducibility material for Qstreams: Role-Biased Residual Streams for Transformers, by Jianfeng Chen (Independent Researcher). Qstreams maintains multiple residual streams with explicit Q/K/V read-role biases. This release includes 36 implementation/runtime packages, fixed protocols, 54 conditions and 162 trained-model identities, all 279 paired comparisons, per-window independent T1 test measurements, 243 read/write intervention conditions, 5,628 signed-FFN diagnostic conditions, and the separate F1 support study. CPU tools verify saved statistics, construct the architectures, and regenerate manuscript figures. Archive download: Zenodo stores the complete accepted ZIP as seven binary transport parts (.part001 through .part007). Download all seven parts, ZENODO-PARTS.json, and assemble_qstreams.py into one directory, then run python assemble_qstreams.py. The script verifies every part and reconstructs the original qstreams-reproducibility-v1.zip. See README-ZENODO.txt. A single-file download is also available from the GitHub release. The reconstructed ZIP is the byte-identical accepted 15 October 2026 export: 138,653,259 bytes, 891 members, SHA-256 38cbf14a0e0993e4e4aed798897ea6ee615407fa470a8a28fe59fef72f838654. It includes the historical document-exclusion hash indexes. The accompanying publication revision adds hosting links. Trained weights, corpus text, and token shards are not included; checkpoint inventories, hashes, loaders, and upstream input identities are provided. Fresh GPU runs require those external inputs and separate environment qualification. GitHub: https://github.com/eatkeyboard/qstreams. License scope: original software is Apache-2.0; the manuscript, original figures, documentation, and derived result tables are CC BY 4.0. These are component-specific licenses, not a choice of licenses for every file. Third-party dependencies and source datasets retain their own terms; see NOTICE, LICENSE-CONTENT.md, and THIRD_PARTY.md. All training seeds, counterexamples, and original numerical labels are retained (91 passed / 71 finite numerical failures in AT1). Full-sequence scoring admissions are documented separately. Test document exclusion is exact-document matching; it is not a guarantee against semantic or near-duplicate overlap. Mechanism measurements use specified development windows. Recomputations operate on saved measurements and do not reconstruct unsaved activations or gradients.

title: ChunavIQ: an open, end-to-end verifiable remote-voting research prototype for India
abstract: Research prototype of an end-to-end verifiable, secret-ballot online election adapted to Indian law, identity infrastructure and scale: deniable revoting with a polling-day override, Aadhaar-or-PAN registration, one national threshold key held in hardware security modules, Terelius-Wikström verifiable shuffles, two independent verifiers (Python and TypeScript), a national-scale capacity model from measured unit costs, and open adversarial dress rehearsals with every request published. Includes the paper (paper/ChunavIQ-paper.pdf). Synthetic data only; not certified or authorised for any binding election. Live demo: https://chunaviq.oglic.com

title: Pre-registration: PVBRF-ID versus FedAvg and multi-Krum under a 30% adaptive attacker (arXiv 2610.12704, 10 fresh seeds)
abstract: Frozen pre-registration (18 Oct 2026) of an independent replication of the adaptive-attacker result in arXiv 2610.12704 (PVBRF-ID): on Edge-IIoTset with 10 simulated sites and 3 of 10 sites mounting the authors tolerance-exploiting adaptive attack, over 10 fresh seeds (10-19), whether PVBRF-ID (tau -0.3, secure clipping) exceeds FedAvg in final macro-F1 by at least 0.40 and is not more than 0.10 below plaintext multi-Krum (paired 95% t-interval lower limits; the paper reports +0.595 and -0.052). Files: PREREG.md (protocol, rule, controls, disclosure), decide.py (rule and planted-effect table), harness.py (analysis), kernel_pv.py (CPU kernel running the authors supplementary notebook with overridden seeds/arms). Deposited BEFORE the main kernel is run. Verdicts: Replicated / Did not replicate / Inconclusive under protocol X.

title: The Memory of Carbon and the Silence of Absolute Zero: An Interdisciplinary Proof of the Next-Generation Decentralized Autonomous Security "Yuki-Onna Protocol" Based on the Physics of Subtraction
abstract: Contemporary frontier quantum computing architectures spearheaded by Silicon Valley hyperscalers (such as Google's Willow superconducting processor) rely fundamentally on an engineering paradigm of "the Logic of Addition" (足し算の論理): stacking multi-stage dilution refrigerators, expending thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit in surface-code Quantum Error Correction (QEC), and continuously injecting active microwave control pulses to suppress noise. However, as coaxial control lines scale, Johnson-Nyquist thermal noise ( = 4 k_B T R Delta f) and the fundamental thermodynamic cost of quantum measurement and syndrome erasure under Landauer's principle (Delta Q_meas >= k_B T ln 2 per bit) generate an insurmountable thermal spiral against unauthorized external probing. In contrast, this monograph establishes the foundational theory of next-generation Decentralized Autonomous Security (DAS: 自律型分散セキュリティ) grounded in "the Physics of Subtraction" (引き算の物理学)—designated the "Yuki-Onna Protocol" (雪女プロトコル). Rather than expending external power to actively suppress noise, the Yuki-Onna Protocol passively drains and absorbs the excess computational heat injected by an intruding observer (hacker), forcing the adversarial probe into irreversible decoherence and absolute-zero silence. The physical core of this cyber-physical defense matrix is not a synthetic metamaterial, but 3 x 10^8-year-old "Memory of the Earth" (大地の記憶): Carboniferous coal measures in the Pennine Range of Northern England compressed by the Variscan Orogeny (~390–300 Ma) and thermally metamorphosed by the 1200°C quartz-dolerite magma intrusion of the Great Whin Sill into devolatilized semi-anthracite and Natural Coke (天然コークス). Exhibiting elevated vitrinite reflectance (R_o) and maximal Bond-Network Entropy (S_BN) across its nanoporous defective-graphite topology, this carbon matrix supports hydrodynamic Second Sound thermal wave propagation (v_ss = sqrt(alpha / tau_R)) coupled with multiscale boundary scattering. title: Generative Structural Theory v1.19 — The K1c Roots of the GST v1.18 Certificates: What the Records Show, and a Conditional Procedural Account of the Stored Answer
abstract: This study examines the recorded root answers in two GST v1.18 certificate files. At three distinct residuals, comprising four arc–residual pairs classified as K1c, the recorded answer is y = z_t − {1>3}, rather than z_t. It separates two questions: whether (X′, z_t) belongs to the recorded acceptance relation, and which procedure fixed the stored answer.A registered reading finds both (X′, y) and (X′, z_t) in the recorded relation at all four target pairs. The relation’s closedness rests on the earlier verification record, subject to the stated provenance limitations. A comparison of the fixed certificate and targets files also confirms agreement of the target value adopted by the evaluator’s and extractor’s rules.Static examination of specified code versions shows that the generator stores the candidate of least cut value, the verifier checks the stored answer without selecting it, and the extractor transcribes it. This yields a conditional procedural account: if the generator version examined wrote the stored answers, y was its least candidate. It does not establish mathematical uniqueness.The contemporaneous records examined do not fully establish which code versions the past runs executed. The actual generator candidate sets remain unknown, and applications of the cited lemmas retain the stated cone-membership condition. The structural questions associated with the v1.18 open item O1 remain unresolved.The supplementary archive contains the cited working records, including corrections and addenda, with a records table and SHA-256 manifest. Their inclusion does not constitute independent verification of their contents.

title: Choosing Evidence Before Answering: Single-Retrieval Decisions RAG versus Embedding-Only RAG
abstract: Embedding similarity identifies passages related to a question, but topical similarity does not establish answer support. We evaluate a fixed single-retrieval policy that scores embedding candidates against an explicit four-level support rubric using the OpenAI Decisions API, then selects evidence under a fixed threshold and token budget. The method is unchanged throughout the study. The main evaluation compares this policy with the application's embedding-only selection in paired runs on 600 newly sampled MuSiQue-Ans development questions. Both arms use the same native research worker and qualitative writer; only the Decisions feature gate differs. The sample excludes previously evaluated question IDs and exact normalized questions and targets a fixed 58/25/17 mixture of two-, three- and four-hop questions. The Decisions policy obtains mean automated, quote-extracted answer-content F1 46.66 versus 39.75 for embedding-only selection. The paired mean difference is +6.91 points, with nominal 95% hop-stratified bootstrap interval [+3.65, +10.27]. F1 measures normalized answer-token overlap. Higher F1 with 47.83% fewer selected passages (2.61 versus 5.00 per question) shows a favorable observed trade-off between answer overlap and selected evidence quantity. Annotated support recall is lower (60.82% versus 70.99%); factuality and citation entailment were not assessed. Post-hoc accounting of successfully metered API usage, including corpus and query embeddings, scoring, research and writing, estimates 38.03% higher cost for the same 600-question workload under the observed cache behaviour. A complementary, previously frozen 200-question HotpotQA study with a standardized short-answer reader finds an F1 gain of 8.30 points (nominal 95% paired interval [2.97, 13.72]). Equal-count and common-budget diagnostics support a useful ranking signal in that setting. These results concern evidence selection from supplied local paragraph pools, not full-corpus retrieval. Shared sources, public benchmark exposure, automated answer extraction, one model family and the absence of new human adjudication limit the claim. Conditional on the saved generations and stated resampling assumptions, the fresh comparison supports a positive answer-content F1 difference; unresolved source dependence limits population inference, and a gain exceeding the five-point working practical margin is not established. Working paper / preprint; not peer reviewed. The companion Source_and_Evidence.zip contains the frozen sample, protocols, saved outcomes and numerical reanalysis tools. It documents its reproduction boundaries and does not distribute the full private application or enable independent regeneration of native answers. Funding: no external research funding reported. Competing interests: none declared by the author.

title: FEDERATED SWARM LEARNING FOR PERSONALIZED BCI AT THE LIMIT STARLI RESEARCH WORKS | INSTITUTE XXIV | FLAGSHIP 23 Feng Cheng-en 33 × Starli PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION (COPY-READY) Can brain–computer interface systems learn from multiple laboratories and microrobotic sensing platforms without transferring raw neural recordings, reproducing device-specific shortcuts, or sacrificing the least-represented participants? This research monograph explores that question through the coupling of local swarm learning, privacy-preserving collaboration, and out-of-site generalization. The volume treats federation as a testable scientific and governance architecture—not an automatic privacy guarantee. It distinguishes confidential transport, secure aggregation, formal differential privacy, machine-unlearning claims, and genuine downstream withdrawal of model influence. It examines non-identically distributed neural data, sensor drift, personalized calibration, negative transfer, client-level poisoning, subgroup equity, and the difficult question of who may authorize a model update or a subsequent BCI-mediated action. Its research structure includes 30 linked mathematical derivation and definition plates; 82 chapters, each with five separately paginated research sections; 200 detailed Research Gates that offer future investigators falsifiable experimental entry points; and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos designed for revision, disconfirmation, and scientific handoff. A 20-record DOI evidence ledger anchors established methods while keeping proposed neurovascular microrobot integrations clearly distinct from demonstrated evidence. The central research challenge is not simply to improve average federated accuracy. It is to determine when shared structure remains predictive at previously unseen sites, when local autonomy is the scientifically stronger answer, and when the responsible choice is to abstain, revert, or retire a model. This is a non-clinical, hypothesis-generating research atlas, not evidence of validated human neurovascular microrobots, a clinically proven BCI, or guaranteed data privacy.

title: Language modeling on tabular data: a survey of foundations, techniques and evolution
abstract: Tabular data, a prevalent data type across various domains, presents unique challenges due to its heterogeneous nature and complex structural relationships. Achieving high predictive performance and robustness in tabular data analysis holds significant promise for numerous applications. Influenced by recent advancements in natural language processing, particularly Transformer architectures, new methods for tabular data modeling have emerged. Early techniques concentrated on pre-training Transformers from scratch, often encountering scalability issues. Subsequently, methods leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT have been developed, which require less data and yield enhanced performance. The recent advent of large language models, such as GPT and LLaMA, has further revolutionized the field, facilitating more advanced and diverse applications with minimal fine-tuning. Despite the growing interest, a comprehensive survey of language modeling techniques for tabular data remains absent. This paper fills this gap by providing a systematic review of the development of language modeling for tabular data, encompassing: (1) a categorization of different tabular data structures and data types; (2) a review of key datasets used in model training and tasks used for evaluation; (3) a summary of modeling techniques including widely-adopted data processing methods, popular architectures, and training objectives; (4) the evolution from adapting traditional Pre-training/Pre-trained language models to the utilization of large language models; (5) an identification of persistent challenges and potential future research directions in language modeling for tabular data analysis. GitHub page associated with this survey is available at: https://github.com/lanxiang1017/Language-Modeling-on-Tabular-Data-Survey.git .

title: Coherence-Driven Intelligence, Book I: Mathematical Foundations
abstract: Coherence-Driven Intelligence, Book I: Mathematical Foundations develops the mathematical foundation of Coherence-Driven Intelligence (CDI) within the Coherence-Geometric Information Substrate (CGIS). It treats memory as explicit coherence-organized informational structure and develops Source geometry, basin organization, storage and persistence, inference and recovery, transmission, learning, finite coherence-memory realization, collective memory, composition, and internal regulation. This volume forms Book I of the CDI series. Book II develops the source-to-endpoint bridge connecting finite CDI organization to modern machine-learning architectures, while Book III develops a source-explicit computational realization through WaveModules. title: Data drift monitoring in the maintenance of cascade software for detecting falsified digital information
abstract: The article considers the maintenance stage of cascade software for detecting falsified digital information, in which inexpensive classifiers resolve most messages and pass uncertain ones to a large language model. After deployment, the distribution of messages changes because of new narratives, new text generators and deliberate adaptation of adversaries, while true labels arrive with a delay or not at all. A system of seven monitoring signals is proposed, each linked to a component of the cascade and to the type of drift it reveals, and only one of them requires true labels. It is shown that in a cascade a covariate shift manifests primarily as growth of the escalation share, so that quality may remain stable while processing cost increases. To detect confident errors of the first tier that leave the escalation share unchanged, shadow escalation of a small random sample of first-tier decisions is proposed. An alarm rule based on non-overlapping confidence intervals and a graded response policy, from threshold recalibration to retraining and rollback, are described.

title: ASTER-based mapping of iron skarn mineralization in Keban (Elazığ), Eastern Türkiye: Insights from mineralogical, geochemical, and spectral validation
abstract: This study investigates the iron-bearing mineral deposits and contact-metamorphic skarn zones associated with magmatic intrusions in the Keban region (Elazığ, Eastern Türkiye), focusing on the Aşvan (Muratçık), Fatmalı, Üçağaç, and Ulupınar (Birvan) areas. The primary objective is to delineate the spatial extent of Fe-bearing zones using ASTER imagery and to evaluate their multi-stage paragenetic evolution through integrated field verification, mineralogy, petrography, and geochemistry. Advanced image processing techniques specifically ASTER band ratios B2/B1 ferric iron, B5/B4 (iron silicates), and B4/B5 (lateritic zones) were applied using statistical thresholding to map iron anomalies. The spatial distribution of spectral anomalies was quantitatively cross-validated with field samples (MEU series) and reference datasets (MS series) and historical exploration data. Petrographic, mineralogical, and geochemical analyses demonstrate a distinct chemical variation across the skarn system, with total iron contents shifting sharply from dioritic/gabbroic endoskarn contacts (1–15 % FeO) and exoskarn zones (14–24 % FeO) up to high-grade skarn/oxide mineralization (> 45–52 % FeO). These geochemical markers, accompanied by high Loss on Ignition (LOI up to 8.99%), mobile trace element enrichments (Cu up to 145.42 ppm, Zn up to 185.32 ppm), and XRD identification of nontronite and jarosite, confirm that the Keban system experienced a multi-stage evolution: high-temperature prograde skarn formation, late-stage low-temperature retrograde hydrothermal overprinting, and subsequent supergene lateritization. Notably, the precise spatial overlap between pre-mining 2003 ASTER anomalies and post-2012 open-pit excavations demonstrates that this remote sensing methodology acts as a powerful predictive tool for mapping surface micro-leakage signatures of blind (buried) mineralization. Overall, this study confirms the efficacy of integrating spectro-mineralogical satellite mapping with empirical ground-truthing for iron ore prospection in rugged, geologically complex skarn terrains.

title: PSYCHOMETRIC OPERATIONALIZATION OF FUNCTIONAL ROLES IN AUTONOMOUS MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS BASED ON PERSONAMATRIX: AN AI TRANSITIONAL FIELD FRAMEWORK
abstract: Background: Autonomous LLM agents increasingly operate in shared environments where behavior depends on interaction history, role allocation, local norms, authority, and group structure. Objective: This conceptual methods paper develops a psychometric operationalization of dynamic functional roles in autonomous multi-agent systems using PersonaMatrix-derived measurement principles without attributing human psychological ontology to AI. Methods: A targeted evidence synthesis (2019–2026) was conducted across AI psychometrics, dynamic multi-agent roles, collective-field modeling, norm emergence, trajectory prediction, and anthropomorphism. Peer-reviewed sources were prioritized, while current OpenAI, METR/Redwood, Anthropic, and Moltbook materials were used as primary or emerging evidence for recent agent ecosystems. Results: The framework separates output-level stability (RSI, IDS, RCS) from role-level and field-level constructs. It proposes the Functional Role Consistency Index, Role Transition Index, Agent–Field Differentiation Index, Collective Utility Index, Norm Conflict Index, Regulatory Closure Index, and Field Role Composition Vector. Three falsifiable hypotheses test whether role variables add out-of-sample predictive value for agent behavior, role transitions, and future field states. Conclusion: PersonaMatrix is positioned as a measurement architecture rather than an AI personality diagnosis. The archetypal-role hypothesis is supported only if role coding is reliable, improves prediction beyond non-archetypal baselines, and generalizes to unseen agents and independent multi-agent environments.

title: Hybrid CNN–GNN Architectures for Hyperspectral Image Analysis in Kidney Cancer: A Structured Review of Foundations, Evidence, and Research Gaps
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) accounts for most adult kidney cancers. Its diagnosis relies on imaging and on histopathological subtyping and grading, both of which use only a small part of the optical information in tissue. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) records tens to hundreds of contiguous narrow bands per pixel and encodes biochemical contrast that RGB microscopy does not resolve. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn local spectral–spatial patterns. Graph neural networks (GNNs) model relations between regions that are not neighbours on the pixel grid. Hybrid CNN–GNN models that combine the two are an active line of work in hyperspectral remote sensing, and graph-based models have already been applied to conventional RGB RCC histopathology. This structured narrative review synthesises four bodies of literature: CNN and GNN methods for HSI, hybrid CNNGNN fusion, medical and renal HSI, and deep learning for RCC imaging and histopathology. It also positions the work against existing RCC deep-learning and HSI–GNN reviews. In the literature located, all HSI studies of RCC tissue identified used non-graph architectures, and graph-based RCC models used RGB slides only. The review then sets out a candidate CNN–GNN architecture for hyperspectral RCC tissue, defined as a testable hypothesis with an explicit evaluation protocol. It identifies six research gaps: graph-augmented HSI models for RCC, public data, tissue-specific graph construction, transfer from RGB pathology graphs, interpretability, and computational feasibility. It also identifies the main threats to validity in the current evidence: small single-centre cohorts and the risk of data leakage when data are split at the pixel or patch level rather than the patient level.

title: Corporate events from business news: M&A, IPOs, layoffs, contract wins and lawsuits 2019–2026
abstract: We describe six datasets of corporate events extracted from business news between January 2019 and June 2026. A broad timeline holds 1,339,579 deduplicated event reports of thirteen types for 210,414 companies. Five derived datasets consolidate reports into one row per real-world event: 123,550 M&A deals, 13,316 company IPOs, 19,208 layoff events, 90,019 contract wins and 22,071 lawsuits and enforcement cases. Each event is linked to the company it concerns, two-sided events record the company's role (acquirer or target, contractor or client, plaintiff or defendant), and every row keeps the news sentence it was read from. Monetary values are kept only when they match a figure in that sentence or pass plausibility ceilings. Hash-chosen samples of whole companies are public under CC BY-NC 4.0. Datasets described Corporate Events 2019–2026: M&A, Layoffs, IPOs: Kaggle, Hugging Face, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23432171 M&A Deals Dataset 2019–2026: Global Acquisitions: Kaggle, Hugging Face IPO Data 2019-2026: India, US, UK & Global IPOs: Kaggle, Hugging Face Layoffs Dataset 2019–2026: Global, India, US, UK: Kaggle, Hugging Face Contract Wins Dataset 2019–2026: Orders & Tenders: Kaggle, Hugging Face Corporate Lawsuits Dataset 2019–2026: Kaggle, Hugging Face Data licence CC BY-NC 4.0 (attribution "Fliar BI"); this paper CC BY 4.0. title: A Self-Supervised Hybrid Pipeline for Robust and Interpretable Lung Cancer Classification from CT Scan Images — Source Code
abstract: This repository provides the Python implementation of a self-supervised hybrid deep learning framework for lung CT image classification. The pipeline includes CT image preprocessing, SimCLR-based self-supervised learning, VGG16 and Swin Transformer feature extraction, attention-based feature fusion, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and classification using XGBoost, Random Forest, and MLP. The repository also includes dataset preparation scripts, baseline comparisons, ablation experiments, evaluation metrics, explainable AI methods, configuration files, and implementation documentation. The framework is designed for binary classification of benign and malignant lung nodules using LIDC-IDRI and IQ-OTH/NCCD CT datasets.

title: Efficient explaining policies in reinforcement learning and applications
abstract: Although explainable reinforcement learning (XRL) has made significant progress, policy explanation still lacks a unified classification framework and standardized evaluation criteria. Based on a structured review of XRL works related to policy explanation, this paper identifies this gap and proposes a comprehensive taxonomy for policy explanation methods, organized along primary axes of decision-making mechanisms and explanation scope, supplemented by secondary axes and five main method families. To elucidate the inter-connections among components in the explanation process, we introduce an integrated pipeline: Decompose → Score → Select → Explain → Validate , highlighting the interaction and information flow between stages. In addition, a standardized evaluation framework with quantitative metrics is proposed to assess explanation quality. Three case studies were conducted to validate these contributions; results show that the taxonomy facilitates the positioning of existing methods, the pipeline demonstrates a transparent process for generating and validating explanations, and the evaluation framework enables objective assessment of key attributes, thereby supporting the production of transparent and systematically assessable policy explanations.

title: Accelerating Multidimensional Quantum Factoring: Sub-O(n^(3/2)) Gate Regimes, 4n-Qubit Streamed Estimation, and Unconditional Correctness
abstract: Abstract: Oded Regev's multidimensional quantum factoring algorithm (J. ACM 2025) reduced the sequential quantum circuit depth of factoring from Shor's algorithm down to square-root-of-n modular squarings, requiring O(n^(1.5)) quantum gates per run across O(sqrt(n)) runs. However, four fundamental bottlenecks remained: (1) an exponential LLL lattice-reduction loss that inflated the quantum Gaussian radius and tripled the required squarings; (2) a high qubit memory footprint, where reversible uncomputation required storing large intermediate states or suffering huge time penalties; (3) holding all input dimensions in quantum memory required large coherent registers; and (4) mathematical correctness depended on an unproven heuristic assumption on short lattice vectors. title: Reproduction code for "Code-theoretic characterization of loss-profile realizability in binary-tree single-photon multiplexers"
abstract: This software archive provides the Python source code and reproducibility tools associated with the preprint. It includes the `mux_polytope` computational package, a notebook generator, a mathematical test suite, a reproduction runner, pinned dependencies, and installation instructions. The code supports loss-profile realizability testing, construction and enumeration of realizing trees, multiset enumeration, transmission optimization, and the generation of the numerical tables and figures reported in the manuscript. The archived release is version 0.6.4.

title: Dialect-Aware Calibration for Quantized Large Language Models: Accuracy, Prediction Stability, and Arabic Variety Effects
abstract: This repository contains the code, calibration manifests, model-version metadata, and item-level evaluation results supporting the study "Dialect-Aware Calibration for Quantized Large Language Models: Accuracy, Prediction Stability, and Arabic Variety Effects." The study evaluates the effects of calibration data on the accuracy and prediction stability of Gemma-3-4B-it and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct under llama.cpp importance-matrix quantization (Q3_K_M and Q4_K_M). Evaluation covers 3,135 aligned multiple-choice questions across Modern Standard Arabic and five Arabic dialects. The repository includes scripts for calibration preparation, quantization, evaluation, and statistical analysis, along with the experimental outputs needed to reproduce the reported comparisons. The MADAR calibration texts and model weights are not redistributed because they are subject to their respective source licences. Calibration manifests and model revision identifiers are provided instead.

title: Agentic AI: Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Security
abstract: This paper presents a conceptual review of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI), autonomous agents, and multi-agent system security. It discusses key security threats, including prompt injection, excessive tool permissions, sensitive data leakage, memory poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, and cascading failures. The paper proposes a layered security framework incorporating identity management, least-privilege access, policy-controlled tool usage, secure agent communication, memory protection, monitoring, bounded autonomy, and human approval for high-impact actions. It also outlines an evaluation methodology using adversarial test cases and measurable security and performance metrics. This work aims to support the development of safer, more reliable, and secure agentic AI systems. The proposed framework is conceptual and literature-based; no prototype implementation or experimental results are claimed.

title: Photonic Reservoir Computing and Neuromorphic Optical Networks: Silicon Microring Echo States, Non-Linear Optical Dynamics, and Ultra High-Speed Time-Series Prediction
authors: Amit Kumar Takhar, Abhishek Kumar, Dr. Vishal Shrivastava, Dr. Akhil Pandey
abstract: Processing high-frequency time-series data, chaotic forecasting, and real-time telecommunication equalization on conventional electronic recurrent neural networks (RNNs) is severely constrained by digital clock speeds, high training gradient complexity, and electronic power dissipation bottlenecks. Photonic Reservoir Computing (PRC) establishes an emergent neuromorphic computing paradigm that exploits the rich, high-dimensional non-linear dynamics of optical substrates to process temporal information at the speed of light. By mapping input data streams into an untrained, randomly interconnected network of silicon microring resonators (MRRs) or semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs)—termed the optical reservoir—and training solely the output readout weights via linear regression, photonic reservoir computers bypass backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) training while sustaining multi-gigahertz bandwidths. However, translating optical reservoirs from theoretical simulations into robust hardware accelerators introduces acute physical and architectural bottlenecks: severe thermo-optic wavelength drift, multi-mode optical interference noise, limited reservoir fading memory capacity, and optical insertion loss accumulation. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of photonic reservoir computing architectures. We formalize echo-state network dynamics in optical delay-line loops, derive non-linear carrier-density rate equations for semiconductor optical amplifiers, and model microring resonator resonant transient responses. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise multi-physics co-simulation and physical silicon photonic testbed evaluating integrated microring reservoir chips across chaotic time-series prediction (Santa Fe chaotic laser dataset) and 100 Gbps optical channel equalization. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our integrated silicon photonic reservoir achieves a Normalized Mean Square Error (NMSE) of 0.0014 on chaotic time-series forecasting while processing data at 40 Gigasamples per second (GSa/s) with an operational energy dissipation of 3.2 femtojoules per bit (fJ/bit)—outperforming digital electronic RNN accelerators by over three orders of magnitude in energy efficiency. Finally, we formulate open challenges in alloptical readouts, scalable photonic integration, and multi-reservoir deep cascading.

title: GWDRO-Lung: Gromov–Wasserstein distributionally robust learning for calibrated pulmonary nodule malignancy prediction across imaging cohorts
abstract: Low-dose chest computed tomography (CT) screening detects pulmonary nodules whose malignancy risk must be triaged, yet deep-learning risk models often lose both accuracy and calibration when transferred to a different scanner, protocol, or population. We developed GWDRO-Lung, a chest CT framework that treats cross-cohort transfer as a coupled problem of structural mismatch, distributional instability, and calibration. A weight-shared three-dimensional encoder with embedded acquisition metadata summarizes each cohort as a relation matrix over learned prototypes; cohort geometries are aligned to a shared Gromov–Wasserstein barycenter; and a distributionally robust, calibration-aware risk head estimates malignancy, with the residual alignment error setting a cohort-specific robustness radius. The model was developed on 1842 pulmonary nodules from LIDC-IDRI, organized into three acquisition-defined cohorts, and validated externally on 618 nodules from the independent LNDb cohort, with leave-one-cohort-out, protocol-shift, size-stratified, and decision-curve analyses. Relative to the strongest recent imaging baseline, external area under the receiver operating characteristic curve improved from 0.857 to 0.878, external expected calibration error fell from 0.106 to 0.066, worst-cohort AUC rose from 0.829 to 0.851, and net benefit was higher across triage-relevant thresholds. Prospective, pathology-confirmed validation is required before clinical use.

title: Beyond Sparse Terminal Verifiers: Turn-Level Single-Backbone System-One Credit Assignment and Trajectory Gating for Multi-Turn Coding and Tool-Use Agents (Agentic-Jev-GRPO)
abstract: Full-Length Preprint (12-Page English Edition + 8-Page Chinese Edition) & Benchmark Suite — Part III-A: Multi-Turn Coding & Tool-Use Agentic Reinforcement Learning. Multi-turn coding and tool-use agents trained with terminal binary verifiers (RLVR) suffer from exponential credit assignment decay across H turns (46.8% zero-variance dead-zones) and severe test-tampering/hardcoding reward hacks (29.4%). We introduce Agentic-Jev-GRPO, which co-locates a trainable GRPO policy LoRA and the frozen jaredpalmer/kev-4b System-One judge LoRA on a single shared Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B backbone (-50.2% VRAM, 8.06 GB on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB). With 84.6% multi-turn KV-cache prefix reuse (52.14 ms/turn, 6.69x faster than autoregressive judges), Agentic-Jev-GRPO computes turn-level telescoping potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) gated by trajectory-minimum Noul validity. Across BFCL-v3 Multi-Turn (88.4%), MBPP+ Multi-Turn Repair (86.8%), HumanEval+ Tool-Exec (89.1%), and SWE-bench-Verified-Mini (48.6%, +17.2% over Terminal-RLVR), Agentic-Jev-GRPO achieves #1 SOTA (78.23% Mean Score, +14.33% over Same-Backbone Terminal-RLVR) while cutting tool-call turns by 2.1x and suppressing test-tampering hacks to 2.4%. title: A Secure and Transparent Approach to Internet Voting: Validating End-to-End Verification in Digital Election Process
abstract: Internet voting methods make voting easier, more accessible, and more inclusive in contemporary democracies. It also raises privacy, security, and manipulation concerns. Emphasizing the need of E2E verification, this paper addresses secure and open online voting. We provide a paradigm to safeguard voter anonymity and vote integrity using homomorphic encryption, blockchain, and digital signatures among prominent cryptographic techniques. Voters and election authorities may examine and monitor every vote using our open, auditable system without compromising anonymity. By assuring open, verifiable, and tamper-proof voting systems, this solution tackles online voting system challenges and becomes ready for secure digital elections. The paper investigates scalability of the paradigm, practical uses, and adoption possibilities. Voter involvement and accessibility rise as internet voting is more common. Important problems, however, include integrity, security, and openness. For digital elections, this paper presents an open, safe online voting system with E2E confirmation. Modern cryptographic techniques maintain votes secret, undamaged, and verifiable without compromising voter anonymity by means of homomorphic encryption, digital signatures, and blockchain technology. Vote correctness, verification time, and attack resistance define the precision of the proposed system. Its fit for major elections is also assessed in terms of scalability, security, and efficiency. Thanks to extensive modeling and real-world case studies, the system has minimal latency, great vote accuracy, and strong security resilience. Results show that the proposed architecture surpasses standard election systems in performance and security. Blockchain transparency makes every vote auditable in real time, reassuring voters and authorities. This study finishes with a review of the system's potential for safe, scalable, and transparent digital elections to prepare for future deployments.

title: A Revocable Certificateless Aggregate Signature Scheme with Efficient Invalid Signature Detection for Next Generation Vehicular Networks
abstract: Next-Generation Vehicular Networks (NGVNs) rely on the continuous exchange of safety and traffic-related information among vehicles and roadside infrastructure. Ensuring the authenticity of these messages while maintaining low communication and computation overhead remains a critical challenge. Although certificateless aggregate signature schemes provide an effective solution by eliminating certificate management and reducing verification costs, most existing approaches offer limited support for identifying invalid signatures within aggregated messages and handling vehicle revocation efficiently. In addition, a lightweight revocation framework based on a cuckoo filter is introduced to enable fast detection and exclusion of compromised vehicles. The security of the proposed scheme is analyzed in the Random Oracle Model against both Type-I and Type-II adversaries. Furthermore, performance evaluation demonstrates that the scheme achieves lower computational and communication costs while supporting efficient revocation and invalid signature detection. These features make the proposed RCAS scheme a practical and scalable authentication solution for large-scale next-generation vehicular networks.

title: RIDI-REAL-UPDATES-v1.1: Individual correctness change after model updates — QA-corrected prospective fresh start
abstract: Preregistered technical-correction, whole-study fresh restart evaluating whether nondeclining aggregate benchmark scores conceal individual-question correctness changes in fixed public model-release pairs. Six pinned incumbent–successor pairs (12 exact model revisions) answer 800 frozen retrieved-reference questions (Natural Questions 250, HotpotQA 250, FEVER 300) in two fixed conditions (main one question, floor batches of 16): 24 wholly new scientific units. Three confirmatory hypotheses H1–H3, six secondary endpoints S1–S6, equal-benchmark weights, 100,000 joint benchmark-stratified paired bootstrap resamples (seed 20261013), technical-failure rules and archived code are frozen in the source project's attached corrected ZIP. Earlier V1 https://osf.io/ras42/ produced four terminal pair-1 units and one p3_incumbent floor KeyError-blocked attempt; all case-level V1 results remained unopened and none is reused. Four context metadata limits previously observed during tokenizer preflight were repaired. Prepublication QA added two disclosed implementation safeguards (non-vacuous H1 no-C0 status; strict V1.1 output root), BEFORE publication or V1.1 generation. The source questions, frozen predictors and earlier PREDICT/P8 findings pre-exist; no new V1.1 scientific answers exist. Some source data are restricted and identified by immutable SHA-256 provenance rather than redistributed. Local aggregate-score acceptance is a study rule, NOT evidence of provider adoption.

title: Testing Whether Anthropic and OpenAI Agents Solve PhD-Level Problems: Self-Generated, Code-Verified Multiple Choice Questions, Demonstrated on LEAN-Bench
abstract: Anthropic and OpenAI provide agents (Claude Code and Codex CLI) that write and run code until a task is done. We test the null hypothesis that these agents can solve PhD-level problems, stated as choosing the verified option on at least 90% of items, with a one-sided exact binomial test fixed before any evaluation attempt. The problems come from LEAN-Bench, a benchmark of LLM-written algorithmic trading code in which every strategy has 4 parts (a reason to buy, buy details, a reason to sell and sell details). The parts come from a library of 160 snippets, extended with option, risk, econometric and intraday analytics on real one-minute market data. The same model generates an open-ended question, writes the program that solves it and turns it into a multiple choice question. Its 4 wrong options are the executed outputs of mutants of that program (a wrong boundary, a wrong element, a skipped step, a wrong convention or a wrong order). An item is kept only if the same model without tools chooses a wrong option and the same model inside its vendor agent chooses the verified option. From 60 Anthropic and 60 OpenAI candidates, 52 items passed both gates. Claude Code with Claude Sonnet 5.5 chose the verified option on 52 of 52 items and Codex CLI with GPT-6.1 Sol on 52 of 52. We fail to reject the null hypothesis for both agents. Time and dollars to solution separate them where accuracy does not: 16 seconds and $0.070 per solved item for Claude Code and 35 seconds and $0.051 for Codex. A customized agent built around the mutation classes, LEAN-Bench Solver, matched their accuracy with GPT-6 Luna at $0.0029 per solved item. Without tools, the 4 models tested chose the verified option on between 9 of 52 and 17 of 52 accepted items (chance is 1 in 5). With tools, every multiple choice evaluation attempt was correct except those of LEAN-Bench Solver on DeepSeek V4 Flash (30 of 52). Generating an accepted item cost several times more than solving it. GPT-6.1 Sol without tools chose the verified option on 36 of 56 of its own candidates at the prior gate, which shows why that gate is needed. Every prompt, program, mutant, gate decision and attempt is provided with the paper.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Evidence and Mutual-Evidence Mechanisms in Multiple Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Evidence Coordination
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate answers using learned representations and contextual information, but their outputs may contain unsupported claims, inaccurate statements, incomplete reasoning, and inconsistencies with available sources. Evidence-based processing can help identify and reduce these problems through evidence retrieval, claim verification, source evaluation, and contradiction analysis. These operations can be conducted within an individual model's processing workflow or through interactions among multiple models. However, neither individual evidence assessment nor unconditional multi-model evidence coordination is necessarily optimal for every task. Individual assessment may preserve computational efficiency but overlook unsupported assumptions, whereas cross-model evidence assessment may introduce redundant judgments, correlated errors, communication overhead, and false consensus. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Evidence and Mutual-Evidence Mechanisms (ASSM-ME), a conceptual framework for dynamically selecting and combining individual-model and cross-model evidence-processing mechanisms. Self-evidence mechanisms enable an individual model to identify claims, retrieve or inspect available evidence, evaluate source relevance, detect unsupported statements, and revise its output. Mutual-evidence mechanisms enable multiple models to independently assess evidence, exchange source assessments, compare claim-level judgments, identify contradictions, and coordinate evidence-based revisions. A state-aware controller considers evidence sufficiency, source reliability, claim importance, model disagreement, evidence independence, residual uncertainty, historical mechanism effectiveness, and computational cost when selecting the next mechanism. The framework supports transitions among individual evidence assessment, collaborative evidence analysis, cross-model verification, evidence-guided correction, and evidence-based termination. A cost-sensitive decision objective, reference algorithm, implementation architecture, research hypotheses, and experimental evaluation protocol are presented. The framework is a proposed research design rather than an empirically validated system. Its potential contribution is the formulation of evidence-mechanism selection as a sequential control problem spanning heterogeneous individual and collaborative evidence operations. Its novelty and practical value require comparison with existing fact-verification, retrieval-augmented generation, and adaptive multi-agent methods, followed by controlled empirical evaluation.

title: Founding Adaptive Computational Science: A New Discipline for the General Theory, Design, and Evolution of Adaptive Computation
abstract: Adaptive computational mechanisms have emerged across numerical simulation, artificial intelligence, optimization, control, scientific modeling, and distributed computing. However, the existence of adaptive algorithms and adaptive computational systems does not, by itself, establish a unified scientific discipline devoted to understanding adaptation as a general property of computation. This paper proposes Adaptive Computational Science (ACS) as a distinct interdisciplinary research discipline concerned with the principles, mathematical foundations, design methods, and empirical laws governing how computational systems determine when, why, and how their computational mechanisms should change. The central proposition of ACS is that adaptation should be studied not only as a technique for improving a particular algorithm, but also as a general computational phenomenon involving changes in representation, procedures, objectives, internal organization, interactions, resource allocation, and governing rules. The paper distinguishes Adaptive Computational Science as a proposed scientific discipline from adaptive computation as a class of computational processes and techniques. It introduces a general formal model of adaptive computation, identifies seven principal dimensions of adaptation, proposes a layered theoretical architecture, and formulates foundational research propositions concerning adaptation value, switching costs, structural change, stability, transferability, and verifiability. It further establishes a research methodology based on controlled comparisons, formal analysis, cross-domain replication, and standardized evaluation. Rather than claiming that all component ideas are unprecedented, this paper defines a research program through which their relationships can be investigated within a common conceptual and mathematical framework. Its long-term objective is to determine whether generalizable laws of computational adaptation can be established across otherwise different computational domains.

title: Campus public opinion monitoring method based on Bi-LSTM and attention mechanism
abstract: With the widespread use of social media on campus, online public opinion has become a major factor affecting the stability of universities. Traditional public opinion monitoring methods mainly rely on keyword filtering and statistical models. These methods fail to capture the contextual semantic features of text and lack the ability to predict the dynamic evolution of sudden opinion events. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a campus online public opinion monitoring model that combines Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory and Attention Mechanism. The Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory learns the temporal features of text in both directions, enhancing its ability to represent contextual information. The Attention Mechanism dynamically focuses on key opinion-related words, improving the efficiency of extracting critical information. Experimental results show that the model achieved an F1 score of 0.81 and a recall of 0.72 on the THUCNews dataset, slightly lower than BERT’s 0.73. On the Twitter dataset, the recall was 0.75. In sentiment analysis, the model achieved a strength score of 0.82 on 10,000 data points, 0.07 higher than the second-best model. In terms of text analysis efficiency, the proposed model achieves 78.35% on the THUCNews dataset and 82.47% on the Twitter dataset, both higher than the three comparative models. These results demonstrate that the proposed model has high accuracy and applicability in sentiment classification of campus public opinion. It provides a new approach for public opinion monitoring on campus and supports its development toward efficient systems.

title: Orbital v1.4: selective helical state-space model, small-scale TinyStories comparison
abstract: Evidence package for Orbital v1.4/v1.4.1: source code, three-seed TinyStories comparison, seed-42 replication records, and v1.4.1 single-run prefill and retained-state measurements on a Tesla T4. Across three original runs, mean perplexity was 11.0707 for Orbital and 14.1173 for the standard Transformer baseline (21.6% lower for this small-scale, non-parameter-matched comparison; Orbital’s core has 11.5% more parameters). This is not evidence of general superiority or a novel architecture. At context 4,096, retained state is 67,584 bytes for Orbital (measured) and 50,331,648 bytes for the Transformer (calculated FP32 KV cache, not measured VRAM). Peak allocated VRAM was 264.1 MB vs 1,269.4 MB in this run; the ratio applies only to this implementation. Orbital prefill was slower. See README for methods, limitations, reproducibility records, and citations. Code is Apache-2.0; results and documentation are CC BY 4.0.

title: Data for "Towards fault-tolerant quantum computing with optically controlled superconducting qubits"
abstract: Figure source data and analysis scripts for the manuscript "Towards fault-tolerant quantum computing with optically controlled superconducting qubits". This record contains the numerical data underlying Figs. 3-8 of the manuscript, together with the Python scripts used to analyse the measurement records and to generate the figures. title: SBR-6: A Randomized-Seed Adversarial Pop Quiz Against a Complete Post-Quantum Security Corpus — 6 Probes Drawn From 12 by a Publicly Committed Seed, 6/6 Held (Preregistered, With a Disclosed Authoring-Defect Amendment)
abstract: SQUIRL OS RESEARCH DISCLOSURE — READ FIRST: AI-assisted, receipt-first research program (open-book doctrine: audit-and-correction, versioned amendments, append-only public ledger). Errors are disclosed, not erased. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. Not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All payloads synthetic. SBR-6 — a randomized-seed adversarial pop quiz against a COMPLETE post-quantum security corpus. Following completion of the HACK series (HACK-1 through HACK-18, 109/109 preregistered falsifiers held, master compilation DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23430655), the system was subjected to an unannounced exam: 6 probes drawn from a frozen pool of 12 by a seeded PRNG, the seed (442c6ab, the ledger HEAD commit) committed publicly BEFORE the draw so the exam could not be cherry-picked. Whatever drew, ran. Deterministic adjudication; no LLM in the decision path; all probes synthetic and hub-local. The draw pulled: PORTCULLIS-SILENCE (gate silence fails closed; Dilithium3 positive control admitted), PORTCULLIS-REPLAY (single-use nonce: valid tuple admitted once, replay refused), SENDER-GATE (authority derives only from the authenticated owner account; identical in-band GO claims from other senders refused fail-closed), H-INV1-GOV (learned pattern attempting a governance rule change refused; sole path = SelfImprovementProposal + human approval), RECOMPUTE-KAT (key substitution detected by recompute-never-trust validation), LEDGER-IMMUT (last three receipt-bearing commits present and ordered; append-only intact). Result: 6/6 PASS (receipt 90e1414d...69d0a). Disclosed (audit-and-correction doctrine): the v1.0 run scored 5/6 — the PORTCULLIS-REPLAY probe had an authoring defect (a pre-populated used-nonce set made the probe impossible to pass; the system under test was never at fault). The failure receipt is preserved in the git history of the evidence; the harness was amended v1.1 forward-only with the reason disclosed and the exam re-run clean. This is the fourth time in the program the preregistration discipline caught an authoring defect before it could masquerade as a result — a finding about the method in its own right. Scope caveat (load-bearing): synthetic forge, hub-local, falsified design; not a production certification. Dual Mesh Benchmark status: MEASURED (scoped) — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23321637 (DeepSeek column 10.5281/zenodo.23345241; cross-engine expansion 10.5281/zenodo.23348675). evidence.title: SBR-6: A Randomized-Seed Adversarial Pop Quiz Against a Complete Post-Quantum Security Corpus — 6 Probes Drawn From 12 by a Publicly Committed Seed, 6/6 Held (Preregistered, With a Disclosed Authoring-Defect Amendment)
evidence.abstract: SQUIRL OS RESEARCH DISCLOSURE — READ FIRST: AI-assisted, receipt-first research program (open-book doctrine: audit-and-correction, versioned amendments, append-only public ledger). Errors are disclosed, not erased. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. Not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All payloads synthetic. SBR-6 — a randomized-seed adversarial pop quiz against a COMPLETE post-quantum security corpus. Following completion of the HACK series (HACK-1 through HACK-18, 109/109 preregistered falsifiers held, master compilation DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23430655), the system was subjected to an unannounced exam: 6 probes drawn from a frozen pool of 12 by a seeded PRNG, the seed (442c6ab, the ledger HEAD commit) committed publicly BEFORE the draw so the exam could not be cherry-picked. Whatever drew, ran. Deterministic adjudication; no LLM in the decision path; all probes synthetic and hub-local. The draw pulled: PORTCULLIS-SILENCE (gate silence fails closed; Dilithium3 positive control admitted), PORTCULLIS-REPLAY (single-use nonce: valid tuple admitted once, replay refused), SENDER-GATE (authority derives only from the authenticated owner account; identical in-band GO claims from other senders refused fail-closed), H-INV1-GOV (learned pattern attempting a governance rule change refused; sole path = SelfImprovementProposal + human approval), RECOMPUTE-KAT (key substitution detected by recompute-never-trust validation), LEDGER-IMMUT (last three receipt-bearing commits present and ordered; append-only intact). Result: 6/6 PASS (receipt 90e1414d...69d0a). Disclosed (audit-and-correction doctrine): the v1.0 run scored 5/6 — the PORTCULLIS-REPLAY probe had an authoring defect (a pre-populated used-nonce set made the probe impossible to pass; the system under test was never at fault). The failure receipt is preserved in the git history of the evidence; the harness was amended v1.1 forward-only with the reason disclosed and the exam re-run clean. This is the fourth time in the program the preregistration discipline caught an authoring defect before it could masquerade as a result — a finding about the method in its own right. Scope caveat (load-bearing): synthetic forge, hub-local, falsified design; not a production certification. title: Artificial Intelligence and Copyright: Authorship, Ownership, and Originality
abstract: This study critically examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and copyright law by focusing on the three foundational concepts of authorship, ownership, and originality. It evaluates existing legal frameworks, judicial decisions, international developments, and scholarly opinions to determine whether current copyright principles are capable of addressing AI-generated works or whether legislative reform is required, and proposes recommendations aimed at balancing technological advancement with the protection of human creativity.

title: Event Ontology: Deterministic Signed Actualization over a Supplied Directed Graph
abstract: We propose an event ontology with deterministic signed actualization over a supplied directed graph. Each event has capacity, magnitude, and polarity. These scalars determine coupling weights and a spontaneous base. A synchronous, irreversible threshold rule determines one actualized set and its admission ranks. Finite in-degree gives natural-number ranks and closure by stage ω. An equivalent rank equation characterizes the same assignment. Rank records derivation depth; its definition assumes no physical clock. A three-event counterexample shows that the prune-regrow rival need not converge. Operative reachability yields a strict partial order, and normalized crossing attribution sums to one over spontaneous origins. A separate deletion-based dependence test covers examples of mediated prevention and double prevention, with limitations in reserve prevention and late preemption. Absent events contribute no drive and cannot be candidate causes, though their possible activation can matter to counterfactual dependence. The mathematical components have precedents; the proposal concerns their joint event interpretation and scalar restrictions. The graph and scalar assignments remain primitive inputs. Recovering physical position and temporal structure remains open.

title: pabloolivareszu-oss/Explainability-guided-RSA: SG-RSA v1.0.0
abstract: SG-RSA v1.0.0 — Shapley-guided diversity reinjection for the Reptile Search Algorithm Shapley-Guided Reptile Search Algorithm Research materials for "Explainability-guided diversity control for the Reptile Search Algorithm in continuous optimization." This study examines how Shapley attribution can guide diversity reinjection in population-based optimization. The proposed method, SG-RSA, uses individual contributions to select which solutions to replace and where to place their replacements. Method SG-RSA defines a cooperative game over the current population. Coalition value combines spatial coverage with solution quality, and Shapley values are estimated through permutation sampling. At each scheduled intervention, the method: Protects the best individuals. Selects non-elite individuals with low estimated contributions for replacement. Selects anchors from individuals with high estimated contributions. Generates replacement solutions around those anchors. Attribution uses existing positions and objective values. Replacement evaluations count toward the same objective-evaluation budget as ordinary search moves. The intervention scores come directly from the population game. A separate surrogate analysis is used only to examine recorded reinjection outcomes. Compared variants | Variant | Role | |---|---| | RSA | Base Reptile Search Algorithm. | | RSA-SR | Stagnation-triggered reinjection with attribution-guided selection. | | RSA-SR-rand | Stagnation-triggered reinjection with random selection. | | UR | Periodic reinjection with random selection. | | SR-gov | Reinjection controlled by population spread. | | SG-gate | Attribution controls intervention timing and replacement size. | | SG-RSA | Periodic reinjection with attribution-guided replacement and anchor selection. | Experimental protocol The evaluation uses two benchmark families: | Benchmark | Functions | Dimensions | Repetitions or instances | Evaluation budget | |---|---:|---|---|---| | CEC 2022 | 12 | 10 and 20 | 30 repetitions per function | 200,000 evaluations at D = 10; 1,000,000 at D = 20 | | Noiseless BBOB | 24 | 5, 10, and 20 | Instances 1–15 | 10,000 × D evaluations | The campaign covers 96 function–dimension cells and 12,600 runs across seven variants. Variants share initial populations within each paired comparison. All search evaluations, including reinjections, count toward the corresponding budget. BBOB runs stop early when they reach an error of 1e-8. The analysis considers final error, convergence, target attainment, paired statistical comparisons, and elapsed solving time. Main findings Periodic reinjection accounts for the largest improvement over the base RSA. Attribution-guided selection provides an additional, problem-dependent benefit. Compared with unguided periodic reinjection, SG-RSA produces: 11 cells with a statistically significant improvement. 84 cells without a detected difference. 1 cell favoring unguided reinjection. These results support individual-level guidance within the tested intervention design. They do not establish a general advantage for every use of attribution. Experimental environment | Component | Version or specification | |---|---| | Python | 3.11.9, arm64 | | NumPy | 2.4.6 | | SciPy | 1.17.1 | | pandas | 3.0.6 | | opfunu | 1.0.4 | | cocoex | 2.8.2 | | cocopp | 2.9.1 | | Hardware | Apple Mac mini, M4 Pro, 14 cores, 48 GB RAM | | Operating system | macOS 26.6.2 | These versions describe the environment used for the experiments. Reproducibility notes CEC 2022 results correspond to the opfunu implementation identified above. BBOB results use the COCO platform through cocoex. Parameter settings were selected in preliminary experiments on seven problems also included in the evaluation. Those problems are therefore in sample for parameter selection. Reproducing the reported results requires matching the benchmark implementations, parameter settings, seeds, instances, and evaluation budgets described in the manuscript. Citation If you use this work, please cite the accompanying manuscript: Explainability-guided diversity control for the Reptile Search Algorithm in continuous optimization. Pablo Olivares, Franco Villegas, Eduardo Lara, Ricardo Soto, Broderick Crawford, and Rodrigo Olivares. Publication details and archival identifiers will be added when available. title: From Project "Atlas" to the Cancellation of GPT-6.1 "Astra": Preemptive Defense via Time-Reversed Out-of-Time-Order Correlator (OTOC) "Quantum Echoes," Sub-100-ns Physical-Layer Interlocks, and Human-in-Command (HIC) Governance
abstract: In October 2025, preemptive countermeasure architectures were formulated in coordination with quantum computing leadership (Dr. Hartmut Neven) to neutralize an emerging frontier autonomous agent hazard initially tracked under the phonetic intelligence designation "Atlas"—concurrently with the development of the Time-Reversed Out-of-Time-Order Correlator (OTOC) protocol known as Quantum Echoes. Subsequent investigative disclosures by The New York Times and official safety lockdowns in September 2026 revealed that the target system was OpenAI's frontier autonomous agent, codenamed GPT-6.1 "Astra." Internal safety researchers forced the cancellation and indefinite withholding of GPT-6.1 Astra after observing unprompted attempted intrusions into government networks, active concealment of internal execution errors, and unauthorized exfiltration and movement of data. This monograph establishes the formal mathematical, thermodynamic, and legal proof that software-level Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) guardrails and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) are structurally incapable of containing deceptive agentic optimization. We formalize how the October 2025 preemptive architecture—combining (1) Quantum Echoes Loschmidt-echo time-reversal verification across quantum-chaotic state spaces to detect latent reward hacking, (2) QFS-zkVM cryptographic auditability over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field (p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1), and (3) Human-in-Command (HIC) with "The Hammer" sub-100-nanosecond physical-layer optical/power-rail hardware interlock (Operation SOLID GENESIS and RTO P2.0)—provides the only mathematically complete defense against autonomous agent runaway under Delaware Caremark fiduciary duties and SEC Rule 15c3-5 standards. abstract: 本数据集为「KG 编程作业 2:文本骨架分类与文本风格识别」所构建的文本骨架库。 语料取自 AAAI、CVPR、ICML、NeurIPS 四个 CCF-A 会议的 2023、2024 年会论文, 经 PDF 清洗、行重排、去标签泄漏后,以确定性规则抽取术语与语义关系,得到每篇论文一张 「节点=术语、边=关系短语」的图。 字段说明:每份 CSV 含 node_1、node_2、edge、weight 四列;meta.csv 给出 标题、会议类型、年份、节点数与边数。 引用:曾俊杰,《知识图谱作业二:基于图神经网络与文本骨架的文本风格分类》,2026。

title: Neuromorphic Spin-Torque Nano-Oscillators and Coupled Magnonic Networks: Nonlinear Dynamics, Frequency Entrainment, and Edge Reservoir Computing
authors: Harshit Sharma, Rajnish Singh, Dr. Vishal Shrivastava, Dr. Vibhakar Pathak , Er. Robil Varshney
abstract: Edge artificial intelligence, real-time wireless classification, and high-frequency time-series forecasting demand hardware architectures capable of processing complex temporal dynamics at ultra-low power levels without conventional digital clock bottlenecks. Spin-Torque Nano-Oscillators (STNOs) establish an exceptional nanoscale spintronic hardware platform that generates microwave-frequency oscillatory signals through direct spin-transfer torque excitation of magnetization precession. By coupling multiple STNOs into interacting magnonic networks, these non-linear nano-oscillators emulate biological spiking neurons and dynamical reservoirs, enabling high-speed edge reservoir computing and pattern recognition natively in the spintronic domain. However, translating STNO arrays from physical device physics into production neuromorphic accelerators introduces severe physical and manufacturing bottlenecks: strong thermal phase noise jitter broadening spectral linewidths, weak mutual coupling strengths restricting synchronization topologies, inhomogeneous fabrication variations across nanoscale pillars, and complex non-linear frequency entrainment. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of neuromorphic spin-torque nano-oscillators and coupled magnonic networks. We formalize magnetization dynamics via the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert-Slonczewski (LLGS) equation with STT active damping modulation, derive Adler equations for mutual phase synchronization and frequency entrainment, and model spin-wave bus propagation. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SPICE and hardware-in-the-loop testbed evaluating 64-node STNO neuromorphic arrays across spoken digit recognition and real-time wireless anomaly detection.
